note: The third multi-volume series (RI-LOR03 §2, ≥3), and the book whose author did not go where he says he went. It degrades across volumes in the way RI-LOR03's multi-volume overlay asks for: the first is thin and mostly true, the second is lifted, the third is invented outright and is the most confident of the three. Every geographical error in volumes two and three is checkable against game/data/world — the Border Falls are described from the wrong side, snow is put in Thornmarsh, the Topal is sailed in the wrong direction, and Lilmoth's crane is put at Archon. Nothing in the game says he is lying. It is a popular book and it is in three settlements.

books.title: A Progress Through the Southern Marsh, Volume the First: Gideon and the Blackwood
books.author: Perquin Aldus Vane, Gentleman, of Cheydinhal
books.unreliability: Mostly true, because for this volume he was actually there. It is also the dullest of the three, which is the joke and which he learned from.
books.text:
It is the fashion among gentlemen of my acquaintance to have been somewhere. Skyrim has been done to death. Elsweyr is a fortnight of sand and a great deal of trouble with the water. Morrowind is currently, as everyone knows, unadvisable. I therefore took ship for Argonia, which is not done, and I present the results in three volumes, of which this is the first and the shortest, the reader will be relieved to hear.

One arrives at Gideon. There is no other way to arrive; the alternative landings are Archon, which is a dye-works with a harbour attached and can be smelled from the deck an hour out, and Lilmoth, about which I shall say a great deal in the second volume and none of it kind.

Gideon is a market cross, a toll gate, and a tangle of streets that all go to the same place. The tolls are posted in three tongues, which the Provincial Office is very proud of. Two of the three are Cyrodilic and Tamrielic, which are, I would gently point out to the Office, the same language written twice.

The people. One sees three sorts. There are the Imperials, who are clerks to a man and who will tell you within four minutes how long they have left on their posting. There are the Dunmer, who hold the warehouses along the wharf and who conduct their business in a manner I can only describe as bereaved. And there are the Argonians, of whom there are a great many more than the returns show, because a great many of them are in the water at the edges of the town doing something with poles that no visitor has ever had adequately explained to him.

I attempted to have it explained to me. I engaged a fellow at the market cross who spoke very good Tamrielic and who was, he assured me, entirely at leisure. He took my forty drakes and walked me down to the water and pointed at the poles and said: fish. I said I could see that it was fish, and asked about the arrangement of the poles, which was plainly deliberate. He looked at the poles for some time and then said: fish, in a tone that suggested he had begun to doubt my capacity, and I paid him a further ten drakes for his candour.

On the food. It is rice, and it is very good rice, and it is served with a paste of something that has been buried. I ate this every day for a fortnight and can report no ill effects beyond an alteration in my opinion of Cyrodiil.

On the climate. Everything I had been told is true and none of it prepared me. It is not the heat. Anvil is hot. It is that nothing dries. A shirt hung in a room in Gideon at dusk is wetter at dawn. Paper goes soft. Leather grows things. My second-best boots were consumed, and I use the word consumed advisedly, in nine days.

On the Blackwood, which I entered as far as the third milestone on the eastern road, in a hired cart, in the company of two men of the Ninth who were going that way and who had been paid by the Office to be agreeable to me.

It is a forest that has been put in a bath. The trees are large, close, and grey, and stand in a foot of standing water that does not move and does not smell as bad as one expects, which is somehow worse. There is no undergrowth, because there is no ground; there is instead an enormous quantity of hanging material, ropes of it, from every branch, in a green that I do not have a name for and that no dyer in Cyrodiil could produce for money.

At the third milestone one may see, to the south, a white stone standing in the trees. My escort told me it was called Ceyatatar-Zel and that it was Ayleid, and that it was not entered. I asked why it was not entered and was told, with the particular Legion flatness that I came to know well, that people did go into it, and that this was how it came to be a place that is not entered.

I did not go into it. I record that I did not, so that the reader may weigh what follows in the later volumes against the fact that in this one, at least, I have told him plainly the one time I turned back.

We returned to Gideon by dark. I have since been informed by three separate persons that returning by dark was foolish and by a fourth that returning by dark was the only sensible course, and I offer this to the reader as the most exact account of Argonian travel advice that I am able to give.

The second volume treats of the coast and of Lilmoth, and of my passage down the Topal, which was in every particular the most extraordinary experience of my life.

books.title: A Progress Through the Southern Marsh, Volume the Second: The Topal Shore and Lilmoth
books.author: Perquin Aldus Vane, Gentleman, of Cheydinhal
books.unreliability: He did not sail the Topal. Most of this volume is a pilot's route description, taken from a book and rearranged, and he has reversed the direction of travel without noticing that the landmarks now arrive in an impossible order.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Sails the Topal shore run westward from Archon to Lilmoth and sets the landmarks down in the order one meets them LEAVING Lilmoth — Lilmoth's own fish-drying racks first, on a voyage towards Lilmoth — then announces that the pilots' book has it backwards and that he has corrected it. Keeps the pilots' left ear for the Border Falls on a run made in the opposite direction, and defends it. Describes at Archon a crane with a factor's counting-office built into the foot of the arm, called the drowned crane for the quarter standing in the sea behind it — which is Lilmoth's crane and Lilmoth's rotting quarter (game/data/quests/blackmarsh-coast.json puts Tesh's office at the head of the Lilmoth wharf under the crane arm) — and then reports that Lilmoth has no crane worth the name. No book corrects any of it; the pilots' book is on the same shelf and disagrees without ever mentioning him.

contradicts.on: the order of the landmarks on the Topal shore run

books.text:
I took ship at Archon for Lilmoth, in a shallow-drawing vessel of the local sort, in the company of a pilot whose name I shall not give because I promised him I would not and because he would be ruined by the association.

A word first on Archon, which I have described in the first volume as a dye-works with a harbour attached and which I now wish to be fair to. The harbour is genuinely fine. The great crane at the head of the wharf is the largest wooden structure I have seen outside the Imperial City and is worked by a crew of Argonians who go up the arm of it without ropes in a manner that stopped my heart the first time and the fourth. There is a factor's counting-office built into the foot of the arm, so that the man who buys a cargo sits directly beneath the thing that lands it, which struck me as an admirable economy. The crew call it the drowned crane, on account of the quarter behind it standing in the sea; I did not ask further, the name being self-explanatory. It lifts, I was told, more than anything on the Niben.

We went out on the evening tide, westward and up the coast from Archon towards Lilmoth, and I shall set down the run in the order one meets the landmarks, because it is the only piece of practical navigation in these volumes and because it may serve a traveller. I am aware that there is a pilots' book on this coast which gives the same run in the opposite order. I have corrected it.

One keeps the fish-drying racks on the right until the smell stops. I record this without embarrassment: it is not a figure of speech, the racks run a full half-mile, and the wind off them is the only landmark to be had in the first hour. When one can no longer smell them, one has cleared the shoal.

Then one looks for the three dead trees. My pilot and I had a small disagreement about this, he maintaining that there were two and I, who could see perfectly well, counting three, one of which was lying down. I mention it as an example of how a man may know a coast for twenty years and stop looking at it.

After the trees the shore turns and one loses it, and one must not follow it, the bay it turns into having a mouth and a false mouth which are indistinguishable from the water at any hour. One holds the heading one had at the trees, counts a slow hundred four times over, and the Border Falls come up on the left ear before they come up on the eye. I set down the left ear deliberately, my pilot having said something else and having said it twice, and I would observe that a man who has run a coast in one direction for twenty years may not have considered how it lies from the other. They are heard a long time before they are seen. When they are heard, one is past the false mouth.

From the falls, the black water is on the left the whole way to the ford, and one keeps it there, everything that has ever gone wrong on that run having gone wrong with the black water on the right hand.

We raised Lilmoth in the grey before dawn, and I shall now be unkind about it and I shall be unkind accurately. It has no crane worth the name, which for a customs port of that size I record as a fact and not as an opinion.

Lilmoth is a city that has been left in the water. That is not a metaphor about its administration; the southern third of it, which they call the rotting quarter, is standing in the sea, and has been for longer than the records trouble to establish, and people live in the upper floors of it and go about by boat between the windows of buildings whose ground floors are the harbour. Nothing has been condemned. Nothing has been demolished. The city simply subsided, over generations, and everyone moved upstairs.

The customs house stands open six days in seven, as the Office's pamphlets proudly say. I attended on the seventh, which was of course my only free day, and found a note on the door in a clerk's hand which I copied out and have framed: THE OFFICE IS NOT SITTING. THE OFFICE HAS NOT SAT ON THIS DAY SINCE BEFORE THE PRESENT CLERK WAS BORN. PLEASE STOP LEAVING THINGS.

On the rotting quarter itself I can give the reader little, having been prevented from entering it by a combination of local advice and the fact that no boatman in the city would take me, at any price, and I offered several. I was told that there is a temple in it, and under the temple a well of the sort that these people keep, and around the well a body of keepers who do not speak to the Empire and have not since before the Cohort came.

I did, however, obtain a description from a gentleman of my acquaintance at the wharf, and I set it down here as I had it from him, with the caveat that I did not see it myself.

The quarter is silent. Not quiet — silent, in a city, at midday. The water in the courtyards is clear rather than foul, which is the wrong way round, and I have had no explanation of it that survives a second question. There are three courtyards past the collapsed arcade where the standing water is chest-deep and the buildings around it are undamaged, doors shut, shutters closed, on every floor. And there are no rats.

I have thought about the rats a good deal since.

ON THE CUSTOMS OF THE COAST, WHICH ARE NOT THE CUSTOMS OF THE INTERIOR AND WHICH I SHALL TREAT SEPARATELY IN THE THIRD VOLUME.

The coastal Argonian — the lukiul, as the word is, and I am told it is not a compliment and I am told this by lukiul — is a person the gentleman traveller will find perfectly comprehensible, and that is precisely the difficulty with him. He wears our clothes, he keeps our hours, he signs our bonds, he complains about the Office in the same words a clerk from Anvil complains about the Office. One relaxes.

One should not. I had a conversation at the Lilmoth wharf with a bond-factor of that description — excellent Tamrielic, Cyrodilic coat, a signet — in which I made some pleasantry about the interior and the sort of people who live in it, of the kind one makes about Reachmen at a dinner in Chorrol. He agreed with me. He agreed with me warmly and at length for about two minutes and then he said, in exactly the same voice: my mother is from Thorn.

I have not stopped thinking about the two minutes.

A further custom, which every visitor gets wrong, and which I got wrong four times before it was explained to me by a woman at the crane who had watched me do it. When an Argonian of the coast does not wish to answer, they do not refuse. They answer a smaller question, correctly, and they wait. If you accept the smaller answer, the matter is closed and no discourtesy has occurred on either side. If you repeat the question, you have said, in their arrangement of things, that you knew what they were doing and did it anyway.

I had been repeating questions since the barge put me down.

ON THE PRICES, for the traveller who intends to go.

Everything imported is four times Cyrodiil. Everything local is a twentieth. Paper is worth more than iron by weight and a good lamp cannot be had at any price on the Topal shore because they are all bought before they are landed. Take paper. Take two lamps. Take nothing you would mind losing to the damp, which is everything, so take very little.

We went out again on the third evening. Going up the coast the run is the reverse of coming down and is easier, the Falls being audible sooner and the false mouth being obvious from that side, and I had the racks on my right again by the second morning and knew I was near home.

The third volume treats of the interior, into which I penetrated further than any gentleman of my acquaintance, and of the stone nests, and of what I was shown at the fourth terrace.

books.title: A Progress Through the Southern Marsh, Volume the Third: The Interior, and the Stone Nests
books.author: Perquin Aldus Vane, Gentleman, of Cheydinhal
books.unreliability: Invented entire, and the most confident of the three. He never went inland. The internal evidence is that he has snow in Thornmarsh, a road where there has never been a road, and a ceremony he describes as taking place at noon in a rite that is not performed in daylight.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Snow in Thornmarsh; a two-week overland road into the Deep Marshes; a fourth-terrace chamber at a site whose interiors are solid; a hatching rite at noon. No book corrects him. Argonians asked about this volume are extremely funny about it.

contradicts.on: whether the stone nests have chambers

books.text:
I come now to the interior, of which nothing has been written by any gentleman, and I am conscious of the responsibility.

We went in from Thorn, in the wet season, by the old road, which is not marked on the Office's map and which the Office would do well to mark, being perfectly serviceable for a cart as far as the second week. Our party was myself, two bearers, a guide of the country, and a young man of the Ninth who came for the interest and whose name I withhold at his request.

The first thing that strikes one is the cold. I had not been told. All the accounts speak of heat, and there is heat, but the ground rises out of Thornmarsh onto a shoulder where the air changes entirely, and on our fourth night there was snow on the thicket wall and my ink froze in the pot. I record this because it is the sort of thing that convinces a reader who has been told a province is a swamp that the writer has been there.

On the eleventh day we came to the first of the stone nests, and I shall not attempt to describe the effect of it, and shall then attempt it, as every writer does.

Imagine a cathedral built by a mason who has never seen a cathedral and has been told only the height. It is stepped, in terraces, each smaller than the last, in a pale stone that holds the light after the sun has gone, and it stands in a country that has no other worked stone in it of any kind, and there is no debris, no quarry, no half-finished second one, nothing that suggests it was made rather than placed.

Our guide would not go up. This is universal, I understand, and I did not press him. The young man of the Ninth and I went up alone, by the causeway, which is a stone road that arrives at the third terrace from the direction of nothing at all.

On the fourth terrace there is a doorway.

I am aware that the antiquarian Fals Rethan has written that these structures are solid and that of the dozen he measured, most have no chamber and one is under water. I have read him. He is a careful man and a good measurer and I would only observe that he measured a dozen and there are a great many more than a dozen, and that a scholar who has not seen a thing is entitled to say that he has not seen it and not to say that it does not exist.

We went in about forty paces. The air was dry, which after a week inland I noticed before anything else. The passage is square, faced in the same stone, and slopes down at a shallow angle, and at the end of the forty paces it opens into a chamber which I shall describe honestly: it is empty. There is no carving, no furniture, no inscription, no bones. There is a floor, four walls, a ceiling higher than the passage, and in the middle of the floor a circular depression about two feet across and perhaps four inches deep, dry, and polished by something.

We stood in it for some minutes and then we left, and neither of us spoke until we were on the causeway, and what the young man said when we reached it I shall not print.

On the ninth day after that we were permitted — and I use the word carefully, and I paid for it, and I am not proud of having paid for it — to witness a hatching at a well of the interior.

It was at noon, in an open place, with perhaps sixty of the country people standing in the water in a ring. There is an opened root, and a pool, and the young are brought and put down at the edge, and they go to it as calves go to a bucket. They drink. It takes a long time; longer than one expects, and there is no ceremony at all, no chanting, no priest, nothing whatever that a Cyrodilic eye would recognise as a rite, only sixty people standing in water in the sun watching children drink for the better part of an hour in complete silence.

And then they look up. All of them. And I say without any embellishment at all, and the young man of the Ninth will support me, that they were different, and that the difference was not gradual, and that I have never in my life wanted so badly to be somewhere else and been so unable to look away.

ON THE PEOPLE OF THE INTERIOR, WHICH IS THE CHAPTER THE READER HAS BOUGHT THE BOOK FOR.

They are not what the coast is.

I say this as flatly as I can, because the gentleman traveller who has spent a fortnight at Gideon has met clerks, porters, boatmen and the sort of Argonian who has learned to be agreeable to a man with money, and he has come away with an impression of a courteous, evasive, faintly comic people, and he is going to be very badly wrong the first time he goes past the second milestone.

In the interior there is no comedy and there is no evasion. A question is answered or it is not answered, and when it is not answered nothing is offered in place of the answer — no apology, no diversion, no charming nonsense about fish. Silence, and then the conversation continues from where it was, and you are expected to continue it, and if you go back to the question you have committed the only discourtesy I was able to identify in a whole season.

They are also, and I did not expect this and I record it against my own prejudices, extremely funny. Not to me. Among themselves. I sat at the edge of a great deal of laughter that I could not follow and was several times told, kindly, that it would not carry.

On the government of the interior I can report the following, which is the whole of what I established: there is none. There is no chief, no council, no assembly, no elder in the sense that word has in Skyrim. There are people who are asked things, and the asking is not a right and the answering is not an office, and when I attempted to establish who would decide a matter affecting the whole of a settlement, I was told, by three people, that such a matter would be decided, in the tone of a man telling you that a stone will fall.

I have concluded that they are governed by a habit rather than by an arrangement, and that the habit is very old and extremely strong, and that this is why the Provincial Office has been unable to find so much as a name to negotiate with for three hundred years and will remain unable.

ON WHAT I WAS ASKED, WHICH IS THE PART I HAVE NOT PRINTED BEFORE.

On my last night inland, at the well, an old one who had not spoken to me at all since I arrived sat down beside me and asked me, in Tamrielic, what happens to us.

I did not understand the question and said so.

She said: to you. When you are finished. Where do you go.

I said that we go to our gods, or that we are judged, or that some of us believe we go into the Void, and that the truth is that we do not agree about it and have not agreed about it for four thousand years, and that a man may live his whole life in Cyrodiil without once being asked the question seriously.

She thought about that for a long time. Then she said: so you do not know either.

And I said no, we do not know either.

And she said — and I have written this down more times than I can account for in three years and it does not stop — she said: I am sorry. I thought you had been told and were keeping it.

On the return I fell ill with the fevers and remember little of the last fortnight, and my notes for those days are in a hand I cannot read, and I have not attempted to reconstruct them.

I shall end with a piece of advice for the gentleman traveller, which is the only reason books of this kind are bought at all.

Go to Gideon. Take the coast. Do not go inland. I have gone inland and I am the only man of my acquaintance who has, and I am the poorer by two bearers, one guide, my health, and something I have not been able to name in three years of trying, and the reader who takes my word for all of it and stays on the coast will have had the better of the bargain and the same book.
